OXON HILL, Maryland (CNN) — Crew members of the Maersk Alabama, safely back in the United States after being attacked by pirates last week off the coast of Somalia, recounted their ordeal Thursday.

Navy personnel recovered the lifeboat from which Maersk Alabama Capt. Richard Phillips was rescued Sunday.

“They start firing before they climb, with AK-47,” crew member Zahid Reza said. “I was scared for my life. I was almost close to that. And they tried to shoot me many times,” he added, pointing to his head. “Pointing gun all over. Here, there, in the back.”

Pirates tried three times to board the U.S.-flagged cargo ship before succeeding on their fourth attempt, fellow crew member William Rios said. He added that the groups of pirates were different, though he believes they were working together.

Rios said he was working on deck when he was called back to help lock down the ship. Then, he said, gunshots rang out, and an alarm sounded to wake all crew members and summon them to the deck.

“We went to our training,” he said, declining to provide details. “If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know.”

Watch the crew praise their captain »

The pirates intended to demand a $3 million ransom, Reza said. He said he and the ship’s chief engineer took one of the pirates hostage.

Reza said he persuaded the pirate — whom he described as a young man, perhaps 18 or 19 — to trust him, noting that he is Bangladeshi and the pirate was Somali.

“His name is Abdul,” Reza said. “I told him, ‘Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.’”

He told Abdul he would take him to the engine room to find more crew members. When they arrived, the room was dark, he said, and he did not know the ship’s chief engineer was inside. Reza said the chief engineer tackled the pirate first; then Reza stabbed him with his knife, and the two men tied the pirate’s hands and feet.

Reza said he intended to kill the youth, but the chief engineer told him, “No, we need him alive.”

Watch Reza talk about wanting to kill the pirate »

“He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us,” Reza said. “A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming.”

Rios said he went to the lifeboat where Capt. Richard Phillips was being held to exchange Abdul for Phillips, but the attempt was unsuccessful.

Phillips — who had offered himself as a hostage in exchange for the freedom of his crew — was rescued by U.S. Navy SEALs on Sunday. The SEALs, positioned aboard the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, fatally shot three pirates and rescued Phillips. A fourth pirate was arrested.

“I feel great they got killed,” Reza said. “I am happy.” He said he was proud of the Navy.

Phillips arrived in Mombasa, Kenya, aboard the Bainbridge on Thursday. The crew arrived at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland overnight.

Watch crew arrive in U.S. »

Rios described Phillips as “outstanding,” “extraordinary,” and “a very brave man.” Another crew member, John White, said they were “damn lucky to be alive.”

Rios called for increased security in the Gulf of Aden.

“Put more military to patrol the waterway for us transporting material back and forth,” he said. “... All the countries got to get involved with this.”

Reza echoed that appeal. “I think government should get involved,” he said. “They should think about our safety, yes. ... This piracy is getting bigger and bigger.”

CNN’s Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis, and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.

U.S. Navy personnel retrieved the lifeboat from which Maersk Alabama Capt. Richard Phillips was rescued on Sunday.

Crew member Zahid Reza said the attackers opened fire before they even climbed aboard, using AK-47s. He said he feared he would be killed. “I was almost close to that,” he said, gesturing toward his head as he explained that the pirates repeatedly tried to shoot him. He said guns were aimed everywhere — in front of him, around him and behind him.

According to another crewman, William Rios, pirates made three unsuccessful attempts to get onto the U.S.-flagged cargo vessel before succeeding on the fourth try. Rios said the pirate groups were not the same each time, though he believed they were cooperating.

Rios said he had been on the deck when he was ordered to return and help secure the ship. Soon afterward, he said, shots rang out and an alarm sounded, signaling the entire crew to wake up and report to the deck.

He said the crew relied on its training, but he refused to describe the specific actions they took. “If I tell you all what we did, pirates, they would know,” he said.

Reza said the pirates planned to demand a ransom of $3 million. He also said that he and the vessel’s chief engineer captured one of the pirates.

The pirate, whom Reza identified as a young Somali man perhaps 18 or 19 years old, was persuaded to trust him, Reza said. Reza told him that he was from Bangladesh and that, like the Somali pirate, he was Muslim.

“His name is Abdul,” Reza said. “I told him, ‘Trust me. I am Muslim; you are Muslim.’”

Reza said he told Abdul he would lead him to the engine room, where more crew members could be found. When they arrived, the space was dark, and Reza said he did not realize the chief engineer was inside. The chief engineer attacked the pirate first, Reza said, and then Reza stabbed him with a knife. The two crewmen then bound the pirate’s hands and feet.

Reza said he wanted to kill the young pirate, but the chief engineer stopped him, saying, “No, we need him alive.”

“He was fighting me and chief engineer, to get away from us,” Reza said. “A lot of yelling, shouting and screaming.”

Rios said he later went to the lifeboat where Capt. Richard Phillips was being held, hoping to trade Abdul for Phillips, but the exchange did not work.

Phillips, who had offered himself to the pirates as a hostage so his crew could be freed, was rescued Sunday by U.S. Navy SEALs. The SEALs, operating from the nearby guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, killed three pirates and freed Phillips. A fourth pirate was taken into custody.

Reza said he was pleased the three pirates were killed. “I feel great they got killed,” he said. “I am happy.” He also said he was proud of the Navy.

Phillips reached Mombasa, Kenya, on Thursday aboard the Bainbridge. The rest of the crew arrived overnight at Andrews Air Force Base in Maryland.

Rios described Phillips as “outstanding,” “extraordinary” and “a very brave man.” Another crew member, John White, said they were “damn lucky to be alive.”

Rios urged that more security be provided in the Gulf of Aden. He called for additional military patrols to protect vessels transporting goods through the waterway and said all countries needed to participate.

Reza made a similar appeal, saying governments should take action and focus on the safety of crews. He warned that piracy was continuing to grow.

CNN’s Paul Courson, Virginia Nicolaidis and Dugald McConnell contributed to this report.

*By Staff Reporter*  
*April 2009*

The crew of the U.S.-flagged container ship **Maersk Alabama** has begun describing the tense hours that followed a pirate attack off the Horn of Africa, offering new details about the struggle to retake their vessel, the capture of their captain, and the dramatic U.S. Navy operation that ended with his rescue.

Captain **Richard Phillips**, who was taken hostage by Somali pirates after the attempted hijacking, was freed Sunday when U.S. Navy sharpshooters killed three of his captors aboard a lifeboat drifting in the Indian Ocean. A fourth pirate, who had earlier boarded a nearby Navy vessel to seek medical assistance and negotiate, was taken into custody.

The rescue brought an end to a five-day standoff that drew international attention to the growing threat of piracy in the **Gulf of Aden** and waters off Somalia, one of the world’s busiest maritime corridors. It also renewed calls from shipping companies, seafarers’ unions, and security analysts for stronger protections for commercial vessels transiting the region.

## Crew describes early-morning assault

According to crew members, the attack began when armed pirates approached the Maersk Alabama in a small skiff. The ship, carrying food aid and other cargo, was sailing several hundred miles off the Somali coast when the pirates closed in.

Crew members said they had received piracy warnings and had taken precautions, including posting lookouts and conducting drills. When the pirates approached, the crew reportedly tried to deter them by increasing speed, making evasive maneuvers, and using fire hoses. Despite those efforts, several pirates managed to board the ship.

Once aboard, the attackers sought to seize control of the vessel and crew. But crew members said they quickly moved to secure parts of the ship, with some taking refuge in the engine room and disabling systems to prevent the pirates from operating the vessel.

In accounts given after the attack, crew members described a chaotic confrontation below deck, where they resisted the pirates and at one point overpowered one of them. The standoff eventually shifted into negotiations between the pirates and the crew.

## Phillips taken hostage

The pirates ultimately abandoned their attempt to take the Maersk Alabama and left the ship in one of its lifeboats. Captain Phillips, however, was taken with them as a hostage.

Crew members have said Phillips’ actions helped protect his crew during the ordeal. Some described him as calm under pressure and credited his leadership with keeping the situation from escalating into a mass hostage crisis.

The standoff ended when Navy SEAL snipers, positioned on the USS Bainbridge, opened fire after determining that Phillips’ life was in immediate danger. Three pirates were killed. Phillips was recovered unharmed and taken aboard the Bainbridge, where he received medical attention.

The hijacking has intensified debate over how best to protect commercial ships traveling through the Gulf of Aden, the Arabian Sea, and waters off Somalia. The region has seen a surge in piracy in recent years, with Somali pirate groups targeting merchant vessels for ransom.

Shipping industry representatives say naval patrols have helped but cannot cover the vast area at risk. The Maersk Alabama incident showed that even vessels following recommended precautions can remain vulnerable.

- Better coordination and intelligence-sharing among shipping companies and military forces  
- Improved onboard defenses, including barriers, alarms, secure rooms, and nonlethal deterrents  
- More rigorous crew training for piracy scenarios  
- Consideration of armed security teams aboard high-risk vessels  

The idea of placing armed guards on merchant ships remains controversial. Supporters argue that armed security can deter attacks and prevent pirates from boarding. Critics warn it could escalate violence, create legal complications, and increase risks for crews.

Maritime unions have also called for greater attention to the safety of seafarers, saying crews should not be left as the first line of defense against heavily armed attackers.

Security experts say the piracy crisis is tied to Somalia’s long-running political instability, poverty, and lack of effective law enforcement along its coastline. Pirate groups have operated from coastal communities where central authority is weak and ransom payments have created a lucrative criminal economy.

International naval forces from the United States, European Union, NATO, and other countries have increased patrols in the region, escorting some vessels and responding to distress calls. But analysts say military action at sea addresses only part of the problem.

Long-term solutions, they argue, will require political stabilization in Somalia, prosecution of captured pirates, disruption of pirate financing networks, and economic alternatives for coastal communities.

The Maersk Alabama hijacking marked one of the most high-profile piracy incidents involving a U.S.-flagged vessel in modern times. While the ship and crew survived, the episode underscored the danger faced by merchant mariners working in one of the world’s most important shipping lanes.

For the shipping industry and governments, the attack has become a renewed warning: piracy off Somalia remains a serious threat, and protecting crews will require sustained international action, stronger shipboard security, and a broader effort to address the conditions that allow piracy to flourish.

**INDIAN OCEAN —** A tense standoff between Somali pirates and the U.S. Navy ended in a dramatic rescue Sunday when Navy SEAL snipers killed three pirates holding the captain of the American cargo ship *Maersk Alabama* hostage aboard a lifeboat, U.S. officials said.

Capt. Richard Phillips, who had been held for days in the enclosed orange lifeboat after pirates attacked his vessel off the Horn of Africa, was rescued unharmed and taken aboard the USS *Bainbridge*, a Navy destroyer that had been shadowing the lifeboat.

The operation brought an end to a high-seas hostage crisis that had gripped the United States and highlighted the growing threat of piracy off Somalia, one of the world’s busiest and most dangerous shipping corridors at the time.

## The attack on the *Maersk Alabama*

The crisis began on April 8, 2009, when four Somali pirates boarded the U.S.-flagged container ship *Maersk Alabama* about 240 nautical miles off the Somali coast.

The ship, operated by Maersk Line, Limited, was carrying food aid bound for Kenya, Somalia and Uganda. It was the first successful pirate seizure of a U.S.-flagged cargo ship in roughly 200 years, according to maritime experts.

Crew members later described a chaotic scene as the pirates approached in a small skiff, firing weapons and using grappling hooks to climb aboard. The crew had been trained for piracy threats and quickly moved to disable parts of the ship, retreating into secure areas while attempting to regain control.

Several crew members said Phillips’ actions helped protect them during the attack. He and the pirates eventually ended up in one of the ship’s lifeboats, beginning a dayslong hostage ordeal.

## Crew fought back

Members of the *Maersk Alabama* crew have said they relied on emergency training, coordination and improvisation.

According to crew accounts, engineers shut down key systems, leaving the pirates unable to fully control the ship. Some crew members hid in the engine room for hours in hot, cramped conditions while others worked to prevent the attackers from gaining the upper hand.

One crew member later recalled that the pirates appeared disorganized once aboard the large vessel and were unfamiliar with its layout. Another said the crew’s priority was clear: keep the ship from being taken to Somalia.

At one point, crew members managed to capture one of the pirates, raising hopes for a negotiated exchange. But the situation shifted when Phillips left the ship in the lifeboat with the pirates, a move that ultimately separated the hostage-takers from the vessel and the crew.

## Standoff at sea

The lifeboat drifted in the Indian Ocean as U.S. Navy warships closed in, including the USS *Bainbridge*. Negotiators attempted to resolve the standoff peacefully while the pirates demanded ransom and safe passage.

Conditions inside the lifeboat were harsh. The small craft was enclosed, hot and uncomfortable, with little room to move. Phillips was held at gunpoint as the pirates grew increasingly desperate, according to U.S. officials.

At one point during the ordeal, Phillips jumped from the lifeboat and tried to swim away, but he was recaptured.

The Navy worked to keep the lifeboat under control, eventually attaching a tow line from the *Bainbridge*. That move helped reduce the lifeboat’s movement and brought it within range of U.S. military marksmen.

## The SEAL operation

As the standoff reached a critical stage, Navy SEAL snipers took positions on the stern of the USS *Bainbridge*. U.S. officials later said the pirates were seen pointing weapons at Phillips, leading commanders to conclude his life was in imminent danger.

With authorization to act if Phillips faced a direct threat, the SEALs fired nearly simultaneously, killing three pirates aboard the lifeboat. Phillips was pulled to safety moments later.

A fourth pirate, who had been aboard the *Bainbridge* negotiating with U.S. officials, was taken into custody. He was later brought to the United States for prosecution.

The precision of the operation drew widespread attention and praise, both for the Navy personnel involved and for the crew members who had resisted the hijacking from the beginning.

## Relief and reunion

After the rescue, Phillips received medical attention and contacted his family. His survival brought relief to his hometown in Vermont and to the maritime community, where the incident had been closely followed.

Crew members of the *Maersk Alabama* later spoke about the fear and uncertainty they faced during the attack. Many credited Phillips with helping prevent a broader tragedy, while also emphasizing that the entire crew played a role in resisting the pirates.

Some crew members said the incident revealed the vulnerability of commercial vessels traveling through waters plagued by piracy. Others said it showed the importance of training, quick decision-making and coordination with naval forces.

## Piracy threat off Somalia

At the time of the attack, Somali piracy had become a major international security concern. Pirates operating from Somalia’s coast routinely targeted commercial ships, fishing vessels and aid shipments, often holding crews for ransom.

The waters off Somalia and the Gulf of Aden are key routes connecting Europe, Asia and the Middle East. The spike in hijackings prompted international naval patrols and changes in shipping practices, including increased speed, armed guards on some vessels and stronger onboard security procedures.

The *Maersk Alabama* incident became one of the most high-profile piracy cases of the modern era, later inspiring books, documentaries and the 2013 film *Captain Phillips*, starring Tom Hanks.

For the crew, however, the event was not a Hollywood story. It was a life-threatening attack at sea — one that ended only after days of uncertainty and a split-second military operation.

Phillips survived. The crew made it home. And the world was reminded that even in the age of satellite tracking and global commerce, piracy remained a deadly threat on the open ocean.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a detailed journalistic summary of the 2009 Maersk Alabama pirate attack, including the crew’s return to Andrews Air Force Base, their praise for Captain Phillips, and their request for stronger anti-piracy patrols.
counterfactuals.output:
In April 2009, the U.S.-flagged cargo ship **Maersk Alabama** became the center of an international piracy crisis after it was attacked by Somali pirates in the Indian Ocean, several hundred miles off the coast of Somalia. The incident drew global attention not only because it involved an American vessel and crew, but because it ended in a dramatic U.S. Navy rescue operation that became one of the most widely reported piracy confrontations of the era.

The **Maersk Alabama**, operated by Maersk Line, Limited, was carrying food aid and other cargo bound for East Africa when four armed Somali pirates approached in a small skiff on **April 8, 2009**. Despite evasive maneuvers and defensive efforts by the crew, the pirates managed to board the ship. The crew, however, had prepared for such a possibility. Many members retreated to secure areas, disabled parts of the vessel, and resisted the attackers’ efforts to take full control.

During the confrontation, **Captain Richard Phillips** became the central figure. Accounts from crew members and officials said Phillips worked to protect his crew and eventually ended up in a covered lifeboat with the pirates, who took him hostage after leaving the ship. The Maersk Alabama itself was soon retaken by its crew and later moved to safety, but Phillips remained captive for several days as U.S. naval forces surrounded the lifeboat.

The standoff ended on **April 12**, when U.S. Navy SEAL snipers aboard the destroyer **USS Bainbridge** shot and killed three of the pirates after determining that Phillips’ life was in imminent danger. A fourth pirate, who had been aboard the Bainbridge negotiating, was taken into custody. Phillips was rescued unharmed, though exhausted, bringing the tense hostage crisis to an end.

After the incident, members of the Maersk Alabama crew returned to the United States and were brought to **Andrews Air Force Base** in Maryland, where they were met by officials, relatives, and reporters. Their arrival was emotional and celebratory, marking the end of a harrowing ordeal at sea. Crew members spoke publicly about the attack, describing the fear, confusion, and determination that shaped their response.

Several crew members praised **Captain Phillips**, crediting him with helping save their lives and prevent the pirates from maintaining control of the ship. They described him as calm, courageous, and self-sacrificing under extreme pressure. While later accounts of the incident have included differing views about some decisions made before the attack, the public statements at the time from returning crew members emphasized Phillips’ bravery and leadership during the crisis.

The crew also used their return to call attention to the broader threat facing commercial sailors in waters near Somalia. They urged the United States and the international community to provide **stronger anti-piracy patrols**, better protection for merchant vessels, and more decisive action against pirate groups operating in the region. Their message reflected a growing concern in the shipping industry: commercial crews were increasingly being asked to sail through dangerous waters where heavily armed pirates could strike quickly and far from shore.

The Maersk Alabama attack became a defining moment in the modern fight against Somali piracy. It highlighted the vulnerability of merchant shipping, the risks faced by civilian mariners, and the expanding role of naval forces in protecting global trade routes. The incident also turned Captain Phillips and his crew into national figures, symbolizing both the dangers of piracy and the resilience of sailors working in one of the world’s most hazardous maritime corridors.
